paragraphs: “As God’s my witness, it just comes out! I never used to say it. All my life I said ‘sir’ to nobody. Then the moment I sank into low water, I started saying ‘sir.’ Some higher power did that. I can see you’re interested in the questions of the day. But how could I possibly have roused your curiosity, living as I do where there’s no room for hospitality at all?”
“I’ve come—about that business.”
“What business?” the captain cut in impatiently.
“About what happened between you and my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Alyosha blurted out clumsily.

“What happened, sir? Surely not that? Is it my ‘wisp of tow’ you mean?” He leaned in so close that his knees actually knocked against Alyosha’s. His lips were pressed into a strange, thin line, like a thread.
“What wisp of tow?” Alyosha muttered.

“He’s come to complain about me, Father!” cried a voice Alyosha knew, the schoolboy’s, from behind the curtain. “I bit his finger just now.” The curtain was pulled back, and Alyosha saw the boy who had attacked him, lying on a little bed made up from the bench and a chair in the corner under the ikons. He lay under his coat and an old quilted blanket. He was clearly ill, and from the glitter in his eyes he had a fever. He looked at Alyosha without any fear, as if he knew he was at home and nobody could touch him.
“What! He bit your finger?” The captain leaped from his chair. “It was your finger he bit?”

“Yes. He was throwing stones with some other schoolboys, six of them against him alone. I walked up to him, and he threw a stone at me, then another one at my head. I asked him what I’d ever done to him. Then he rushed me and bit my finger badly. I don’t know why.”
“I’ll thrash him, sir, this very minute!” The captain sprang up again.
“But I’m not complaining at all, I’m only telling you ... I don’t want him thrashed. Besides, he looks ill.”

“And you think I’d thrash him? That I’d take my Ilusha and thrash him right in front of you, to give you satisfaction? Would you like it done now, sir?” said the captain, suddenly rounding on Alyosha as if he meant to fly at him. “I’m sorry about your finger, sir. But instead of thrashing Ilusha, would you rather I chopped off my own four fingers with this knife, here, before your eyes, to satisfy your just anger? Four fingers, I’d think, should be enough to slake your thirst for revenge. You won’t be asking for the fifth as well?” He broke off, his voice catching in his throat. Every feature of his face was twitching and working, and he looked wildly defiant. He was in a kind of frenzy.

“I think I see it all now,” said Alyosha, gently and sadly, still sitting where he was. “So your boy is a good boy. He loves his father, and he went for me because I’m the brother of the man who wronged you.... Now I see,” he repeated thoughtfully. “My brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch is sorry for what he did, I know that. If he can possibly come to you—or better still, meet you at the very same place—he’ll ask your forgiveness in front of everyone, if you want him to.”
“After he’s pulled out my beard, you mean, he’ll ask my forgiveness? And he thinks that will wrap it up nicely, does he?”
“Oh, no! Quite the opposite. He’ll do whatever you like, and however you like.”
“So if I were to ask his highness to go down on his knees before me in that very tavern—‘The Metropolis,’ it’s called—or in the marketplace, he’d do it?”
“Yes, he would even go down on his knees.”

“You’ve pierced me to the heart, sir. You’ve brought me to tears, and pierced me to the heart! I’m only too well aware of your brother’s generosity. Let me introduce my family: my two daughters and my son—my litter. If I die, who’ll look after them? And as long as I live, who but them will care about a wretch like me? That’s a great thing the Lord has arranged for every man of my sort, sir. Because there has to be someone who can love even a man like me.”
“Ah, that’s perfectly true!” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Oh, stop playing the fool! Some idiot walks in and you make us all look ridiculous!” cried the girl by the window, suddenly turning to her father with a scornful, contemptuous look.
“Wait a bit, Varvara!” her father cried sharply, though he looked at her quite approvingly. “That’s her character,” he told Alyosha again.
“And in all nature there was naught That could find favor in his eyes—

or rather, to put it in the feminine, that could find favor in her eyes. But now let me present you to my wife, Arina Petrovna. She’s a cripple, forty-three years old; she can move, but only a very little. She comes of humble people. Arina Petrovna, compose your face. This is Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Get up, Alexey Fyodorovitch.” He took him by the hand and, with surprising strength, hauled him to his feet. “You have to stand to be introduced to a lady. This isn’t the Karamazov, mamma, who ... h’m ... et cetera, but his brother, radiant with modest virtues. Come now, Arina Petrovna, come, mamma, let him kiss your hand first.”

And he kissed his wife’s hand with respect, even tenderness. The girl at the window turned her back on it all in disgust. Over the proud, questioning face of the woman came a look of extraordinary warmth.
“Good morning! Sit down, Mr. Tchernomazov,” she said.
“Karamazov, mamma, Karamazov. We come of humble people,” he whispered again.

“Well, Karamazov, or whatever it is, I always think of Tchernomazov.... Sit down. Why did he haul you up? He calls me a cripple, but I’m not. It’s just that my legs are swollen like barrels, and the rest of me has shriveled up. I used to be so fat, and now it’s as if I’d swallowed a needle.”
“We come of humble people,” the captain muttered again.
“Oh, Father, Father!” said the hunchback girl, who until then had sat silent on her chair, and she hid her eyes in her handkerchief.
“Buffoon!” the girl at the window burst out.

“Have you heard our news?” said the mother, pointing at her daughters. “It’s like clouds rolling in; the clouds pass and we have music again. When we were with the army, we had plenty of guests like this. I’m not comparing anyone, mind; each to their own taste. The deacon’s wife used to come then and say, ‘Alexandr Alexandrovitch is a man with the noblest heart, but Nastasya Petrovna,’ she’d say, ‘is a child of hell.’ ‘Well,’ I said, ‘that’s a matter of taste, but you’re a little spitfire.’ ‘And you need putting in your place,’ says she. ‘You black sword,’ said I, ‘who asked you to teach me?’ ‘But my breath,’ says she, ‘is clean, and yours is foul.’ ‘Go and ask all the officers if my breath is foul.’ And I’ve had it on my mind ever since. Just the other day I was sitting here, just as I am now, when I saw that same general walk in, the one who came here at Easter, and I asked him: ‘Your Excellency,’ said I, ‘can a lady’s breath be unpleasant?’ ‘Yes,’ he answered; ‘you ought to open a window-pane or the door, because the air in here isn’t fresh.’ That’s how they all carry on! And what is my breath to them? The dead smell worse! ‘I won’t spoil the air,’ said I, ‘I’ll order some slippers and be off.’ My darlings, don’t blame your own mother! Nikolay Ilyitch, why can’t I please you? Only Ilusha comes home from school and loves me. Yesterday he brought me an apple. Forgive your own mother—forgive a poor lonely creature! Why has my breath become so unpleasant to you?”
And the poor mad woman broke down in sobs, with tears running down her cheeks. The captain ran over to her.

“Mamma, mamma, my dear, don’t, don’t! You’re not lonely. Everyone loves you, everyone adores you.” He began kissing both her hands again and tenderly stroking her face. Then he took the dinner napkin and started wiping away her tears. Alyosha thought there were tears in his eyes too. “There, you see? You hear?” he said, wheeling on Alyosha in a sort of fury and pointing at the poor imbecile.
“I see and I hear,” muttered Alyosha.
“Father, Father, how can you—with him! Leave him be!” cried the boy, sitting up in bed and staring at his father with blazing eyes.
“Enough of this clowning! Enough of your silly antics that never come to anything!” shouted Varvara, stamping her foot in a passion.

“This time your anger is perfectly just, Varvara, and I’ll hurry to satisfy you. Come, Alexey Fyodorovitch, put on your cap, and I’ll put on mine. We’ll go out. I have something serious to say to you, but not inside these walls. This girl sitting here is my daughter Nina. I forgot to introduce her. She is a heavenly angel incarnate ... who has flown down among us mortals,... if you can understand.”
“Look at him, shaking all over, as though he were in convulsions!” Varvara went on indignantly.

“And she there, stamping her foot at me and calling me a fool a minute ago, she too is a heavenly angel incarnate, and she has good reason to call me one. Come along, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we have to put an end to this.”
And, seizing Alyosha’s hand, he led him out of the room and into the street.
